title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 60
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Waiting Outside the Gate
passages.text:
A. Quarantine is older than any understanding of what it was preventing. Ships arriving at certain ports were required to wait offshore for a fixed period before anyone could land, on the observation that disease appeared among new arrivals within a certain number of days and that those who remained well for longer did not bring it. The practice worked, the reasoning behind it was wrong in every particular, and it is among the clearest cases of a correct procedure derived from an incorrect theory.

B. The fixed period was a guess that happened to be adequate. It was set by convention rather than by measurement of any specific disease, it was longer than necessary for some infections and too short for others, and its persistence for centuries owed as much to administrative convenience as to evidence. Modern practice sets the period from the observed incubation of the particular organism, which is a different procedure that inherited a name.

C. Enforcement always fell unevenly and the pattern is consistent across centuries. Wealthy passengers were released early or exempted, cargo of value moved faster than cargo of none, and the burden concentrated on crews, migrants and the poor — with the predictable consequence that those with reason to avoid detention concealed illness, which is precisely the behaviour the measure needs not to provoke.

D. The economic incentive to under-report has never been solved and shapes the whole system. A port or a country declaring an outbreak faces immediate losses in trade, shipping and travel, and receives no compensation for having reported honestly, so the rational course for any individual authority is to delay. International arrangements requiring notification exist and are followed unevenly for exactly this reason, and adding penalties for late reporting strengthens the incentive to conceal rather than weakening it.

E. What determines whether the measure works is almost never the rule itself. Compliance depends on whether people can afford to comply — whether isolating means losing income, whether food arrives, whether the family is supported — and populations that are supported comply at rates that populations left to manage do not. This has been observed repeatedly and is treated as a new discovery each time.

F. The measure's usefulness is narrower than either its advocates or its critics claim. It buys time when a disease is not yet widespread, is close to useless once transmission is established within a population, and its cost falls immediately on identifiable people while its benefit is a diffuse and unprovable absence. Deciding when to use it is therefore a judgement made under uncertainty about a benefit that cannot be demonstrated afterwards.

passages.title: Taking Nitrogen from the Air
passages.text:
Nitrogen makes up most of the atmosphere and almost nothing can use it. The two atoms in a nitrogen molecule are held together by one of the strongest bonds in chemistry, and breaking it is what stands between a plant and the element it needs most after carbon; the availability of nitrogen in usable form, not its abundance, is what limits growth across most of the natural world.

Some bacteria break that bond, and every natural ecosystem depends on them. They possess an enzyme that performs the reaction at ordinary temperature and pressure, at a considerable cost in energy, and many of them live in association with plants — in root nodules that the plant builds and supplies with sugars, receiving usable nitrogen in exchange. This is why a crop of beans or clover leaves soil richer than it found it, and why rotations built around such crops worked long before anyone knew why.

The industrial process that replaced dependence on them is among the most consequential inventions of the modern era. Combining atmospheric nitrogen with hydrogen under high temperature and pressure over a catalyst produces ammonia, and from it the fertiliser that a large share of the world's food supply now depends on. A substantial proportion of the nitrogen in the average person's body has passed through that process, which is an unusual thing to be able to say about an industrial reaction.

The costs arrive at both ends of the process. Making the ammonia consumes a significant share of global energy production and the hydrogen for it comes mostly from fossil gas; the fertiliser applied to fields is taken up incompletely, and the remainder runs into water, where it produces the algal growth and oxygen depletion that damages rivers, lakes and coastal seas, or escapes as a gas with a strong warming effect.

Efficiency is where the practical gains are and they are unevenly distributed. Application rates in some regions exceed what crops can use by a wide margin, so reductions there cost nothing in yield; in other regions application is far below what would be productive, and the same fertiliser would produce large gains. Moving nitrogen from where it is wasted to where it is scarce would improve both problems, and no mechanism exists to do it.

The prospect of engineering cereals to fix their own nitrogen is real, distant and frequently misdescribed. The bacterial machinery is complex, it is destroyed by oxygen, and the plant would have to build a protected environment and pay a substantial energy cost, which is why the plants that do it are not the highest-yielding ones. It is a serious research programme whose success would matter enormously and is not imminent.

passages.title: Buying on Behalf of Everyone
passages.text:
Governments are among the largest purchasers in any economy, and how they buy determines a great deal that is usually attributed to policy. The rules governing public purchasing exist to prevent corruption and favouritism, they succeed at that better than their reputation suggests, and they impose costs that are rarely counted because the alternative's costs are more visible.

Competitive tendering is the default and its logic is defensive. Publishing a specification, inviting bids and awarding to the best against stated criteria makes the decision auditable and gives an unsuccessful bidder something to challenge, which is what deters the arrangement the rules exist to prevent. The process is slow, expensive for both sides, and biased towards suppliers who are good at tendering rather than at the work.

The specification is where most failures originate and it is written before anyone knows enough. A buyer must describe what is wanted in advance, in enough detail to compare bids, for something that will be delivered over years — and for anything novel, the knowledge required to write that description does not exist until the work is under way. Fixed specifications for uncertain work produce contracts that must be varied, and variations are where costs escape.

Lowest-price awarding is widely blamed and is usually a symptom. Where a buyer lacks the capacity to evaluate quality defensibly, price is the criterion that can be justified to an auditor, so an under-resourced purchasing function retreats to it regardless of the rules permitting otherwise. The problem is the missing expertise rather than the criterion, and adding rules about quality without adding the capacity to assess it changes little.

Concentration follows from the cost of bidding. Every requirement added to a tender process raises the fixed cost of participating, which small suppliers cannot spread over many contracts, so measures intended to ensure quality and integrity systematically favour large incumbents. Public buyers frequently complain about supplier concentration in markets their own procedures have concentrated.

What performs better is known and hard to adopt. Retaining enough in-house expertise to be an intelligent client, contracting in stages when the work is uncertain rather than specifying everything at the start, awarding on assessed value rather than price alone, and accepting that some failure is the cost of buying anything difficult — each requires a tolerance for visible error that public purchasing is structured to avoid.
